newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk court told of police "concentration camp".
newsitem.headline: Turk court told of police "concentration camp".

text.p: Turkish police beat suspects until their wooden batons broke, a witness on Friday said at a murder trial seen as a test of Turkey's human rights record.
Journalist Aydin Aydemir said she saw police clubbing people in a sports complex in Istanbul where fellow reporter Metin Goktepe was allegedly battered to death by police in January.
"We heard sounds of beating and wooden sticks breaking. I didn't see Metin but I saw a lot of people being beaten. I thought the death toll would have been greater," she said.
Forty-eight policemen went on trial on Friday in the southwestern town of Aydin for Goktepe's death in a trial being held under the critical eye of Turkey's Western allies.

Claims of extrajudicial killings and deaths by torture in Turkish police custody are rife -- the Ankara-based Human Rights Association says there were 21 just in August this year -- but it is rare that the perpetrators come before the law.
Aydemir said police rounded up scores of people at random for an identity check in Eyup sports complex after the funerals of two far-left militant prisoner.
"It was like a concentration camp. There were old and young people. Some were picked up while going to the grocers or trying to catch a bus," she told the packed court.
The trial was transferred to Aydin from Istanbul, some 800 km (500 miles) away, a move rights activists say was an attempt to keep the court proceedings out of the public eye.
But some 300 observers, journalsts and relatives turned up at the court room on Friday morning, forcing judge Turgut Yildirim to switch the trial to a large sports hall nearby.
Witnesses and court officials sat on wooden benches hastily laid out in the hall and used a microphone when addressing the court.

"This is a case important for the victim, of course, and also for Turkey," Euro MP Magda Aelvoet from Belgium told Reuters at the court. "Turkey might show with a correct trial that it is serious about respecting law," she said.
Euro MPs have threatened to block hundreds of millions of dollars in European Union aid to Turkey, partly because of Ankara's human rights problems.
Rights group Amnesty International this month launched a worldwide campaign to focus attention on abuses in Turkey, particularly extrajudicial killings, torture and disappearances.
Turkey says Amnesty is biased against it but Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller on Thursday vowed to clamp down on human rights failings.
The Turkish media has given rare prominence to Goktepe's killing.
"They killed my son," Goktepe mother Fadime, 65, told the court referring to the police. Some of her relatives wore tee-shirts with a photograph of the dead journalist printed on them.
The policement charged with the killing were not in court and have been allowed to answer the accusations against them in prepared statements without appearing before the judge.
No formal plea is needed under Turkish law.
Another witness said police piled Goktepe and other suspects onto a bus during the detention.
"I saw Metin on the bus. People had been made to lie down. They were piled on top of each other and the police were beating up everyone," journalist Kemal Ertas said.
"The police were walking up and down on top of people," he said.
